\">\u003cfigcaption>Figure · page 17\u003c/figcaption>\u003c/figure>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Rockall Score is another important scoring system used  after endoscopy.It predicts:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">✓ mortality risk,   ✓ and risk of rebleeding.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The Rockall score combines:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. age,   2. Shock,   3. comorbidities,   4. endoscopic diagnosis,   5. and stigmata of recent hemorrhage.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Higher Rockall scores are associated with:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. increased mortality,   2. recurrent bleeding,   3. and need for aggressive intervention.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Unlike GBS, Rockall becomes more class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>Pre-Endoscopy Rockall Score: Uses only the clinical criteria (Age, Shock,\u003cbr>Comorbidities) before an endoscopy is performed. It is scaled from 0 to 7 points. A\u003cbr>pre-endoscopic score of 0 denotes an exceptionally low risk.\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Complete Rockall Score: Incorporates all 5 parameters following a complete\u003cbr>gastroscopy. It is scaled from 0 to 11 points\u003cbr>\u003cbr>Risk Stratification &amp; Clinical Guidance\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Medical professionals use the final tallied complete score to determine patient placement and\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">discharge readiness:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. Low Risk (Score ≤ 2): Patients have an excellent prognosis (mortality &lt;1%, low\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">rebleeding risk) and can usually be safely fast-tracked for early hospital discharge or\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">outpatient management.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. Moderate Risk (Score 3–7): Requires inpatient admission and monitoring due to a\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">stepwise escalation in rebleeding and mortality complications.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">3. High Risk (Score ≥ 8): Carries highly intensive care needs and a high overall\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">mortality risk (often exceeding 40%–50%).\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">AIMS65 Score\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">AIMS65 Score is a rapid bedside mortality predictor commonly used in emergencies and\u003cbr>ICU settings. It predicts: inpatient mortality, ICU need and severity.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The components are:\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable g/dL\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>I\u003c/td>\u003ctd>INR &gt;1.5\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>M\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Altered mental low\u003cbr>physiologic reserve\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>I\u003c/td>\u003ctd>INR\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>&gt;1.5\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Coagulopathy and impaired clotting with increased\u003cbr>bleeding risk\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>M\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Mental status\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Altered mental\u003cbr>status\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Severe systemic compromise, hypoperfusion,\u003cbr>encephalopathy, or shock\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>S\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Systolic\u003cbr>Blood\u003cbr>Pressure\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>&lt;90 mmHg\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Hemodynamic instability and significant acute\u003cbr>blood loss\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>65\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Age\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>&gt;65 years\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Reduced physiologic reserve and higher mortality\u003cbr>risk\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Higher scores predict:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">✓ worse outcomes,   ✓ longer hospital stay,   ✓ and increased mortality.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Overall Clinical Interpretation of AIMS65 Score\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The higher the: AIMS65 score the worse the overall prognosis. Patients with scores of:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">0–1 usually have relatively lower mortality risk and may only require standard inpatient\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">monitoring if clinically stable.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">A score of: 2 suggests moderate disease severity with increased risk of complications, ICU\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">requirement, and need for aggressive monitoring.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Scores ≥3 are considered high risk and are strongly associated with severe hemorrhage,\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">multiorgan dysfunction, hepatic decompensation, prolonged hospital stays, ICU admission,\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">and increased mortality. These patients require aggressive resuscitation, urgent endoscopy,\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">close hemodynamic monitoring, and often HDU/ICU-level care.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Forrest Classification and Rebleeding Risk\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">In non-variceal bleeding, especially peptic ulcer disease, the:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Forrest classification\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">is used to assess risk of recurrent hemorrhage.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The Forrest system classifies ulcers according to endoscopic appearance.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 20\u003c/div>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">CHILD-PUGH SCORE\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The Child-Pugh Score is used to assess the severity and prognosis of chronic liver disease by\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">estimating liver functional reserve, risk of complications, operative risk, and overall survival.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">It is based on five important parameters: bilirubin, albumin, INR/prothrombin time, ascites,\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">and hepatic encephalopathy, which together reflect the liver’s excretory function, synthetic\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">capacity, and degree of portal hypertension and hepatic decompensation. Higher Child-Pugh\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">scores indicate worsening hepatic synthetic dysfunction, more advanced portal hypertension,\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">p oorer physiologic reserve, and increased mortality risk.\u003c/p>\u003cfigure class=\"note-figure\">\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Illustration associated with page 20\" src=\"data:image/webp;base64,\">\u003cfigcaption>Figure · page 20\u003c/figcaption>\u003c/figure>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable function\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Albumin\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Liver synthetic function\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>INR/PT\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Coagulation factor failure\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 21\u003c/div>\u003cp compromise\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>C\u003c/td>\u003ctd>10–15\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Decompensated liver disease\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">MODEL FOR END-STAGE LIVER DISEASE ( MELD SCORE )\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The Model for End-Stage Liver Disease is an objective prognostic scoring system used to\u003cbr>assess the severity of advanced liver disease and estimate short-term mortality risk, especially\u003cbr>in patients with Cirrhosis. It is commonly used to predict survival, assess severity of hepatic\u003cbr>decompensation, determine ICU and transplant priority, and evaluate the risk of\u003cbr>complications such as renal failure and variceal bleeding. The MELD score is mainly\u003cbr>calculated using serum bilirubin, INR, and creatinine, which reflect hepatic excretory\u003cbr>dysfunction, coagulation impairment, and renal dysfunction respectively. Higher MELD\u003cbr>scores indicate worsening liver failure, greater hepatorenal dysfunction, increased risk of\u003cbr>multiorgan failure, and significantly higher short-term mortality.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">ICU Admission Criteria\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Patients may require ICU-level care if they have:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. persistent hypotension,\u003cbr>2. massive transfusion requirement,\u003cbr>3. respiratory failure,\u003cbr>4. altered consciousness,\u003cbr>5. active massive hematemesis,\u003cbr>6. severe cirrhosis,\u003cbr>7. or multiorgan dysfunction.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">ICU monitoring allows:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">✓ invasive hemodynamic monitoring,\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">✓ airway protection,   ✓ Vasopressor support,   ✓ and rapid transfusion if needed.\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>1. Glasgow-Blatchford Score is mainly pre-endoscopic.\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>2. Rockall Score becomes more useful after endoscopy.\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>3. AIMS65 is a rapid bedside mortality predictor.\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>4. Forrest classification predicts rebleeding in peptic ulcer disease.\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>5. Cirrhotic patients with UGIB are automatically high risk.\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>6. Hypotension and ongoing transfusion requirement strongly predict class=\"note-text-block\">outcome.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 22\u003c/div>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">ENDOSCOPY MANAGEMENT\u003c/h3>\u003cfigure class=\"note-figure\">\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Illustration associated with page 22\" src=\"data:image/webp;base64,\">\u003cfigcaption>Figure · page 22\u003c/figcaption>\u003c/figure>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">After stabilization, hemostatic therapy, and risk stratification, the next major step in the\u003cbr>management of upper gastrointestinal bleeding is:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy is considered the: Gold standard investigation\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">According to the American College of Gastroenterology (ACG), European Society of\u003cbr>Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (ESGE), Davidson’s Principles and Practice of Medicine, and\u003cbr>Harrison’s Internal Medicine, early endoscopy significantly reduces: mortality,  rebleeding,\u003cbr>blood transfusion requirements, ICU admission, and need for surgery.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The main purposes of endoscopy are:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>identification of the bleeding source,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>assessment of bleeding severity,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>risk stratification,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Haemostasis,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>and prevention of recurrent hemorrhage.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Timing of Endoscopy\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The timing of endoscopy depends on:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. hemodynamic stability,   2. severity of bleeding,   3. and clinical suspicion.\u003c/h3>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>According to current UGIB guidelines: High-risk patients should undergo: Urgent\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>endoscopy within 12 hours\u003c/td>\u003ctd>especially if:\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. suspected variceal bleeding,   2. active hematemesis,   3. hemodynamic instability,\u003c/h3>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 23\u003c/div>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">4. or ongoing transfusion requirements are present.\u003c/h3>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Other stabilized patients should undergo: Endoscopy within 24 hours after adequate\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>resuscitation.\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Endoscopy should not be performed before stabilization because severe hypotension and\u003cbr>hypoxia increase procedural mortality.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Diagnostic Role of Endoscopy\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The first major role of endoscopy is:Diagnosis\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Forrest Classification During Endoscopy\u003c/h4>\u003cfigure class=\"note-figure\">\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Illustration associated with page 23\" src=\"data:image/webp;base64,
